rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 and Figures 3-8 report the authors' own model runs (linear quadratic optimal control applied to a state-space soil-crop-climate model) producing hourly irrigation schedules over a 50-day horizon for maize on Panoche clay under five salinity/cost case studies.
rows.notes: The study is purely a simulation/optimisation exercise. Case 1 (section 5.3) reports that low-cost control uses 48 cm of water (30 cm drained) while high-cost control uses 16 cm (2 cm percolation), i.e. the controller reduces applied water when water is expensive, but these are model outputs never compared with measurements from a real field system. The authors note that calibration/verification of the crop model was done in earlier work (Protopapas and Bras 1988) and only check the linearisation against the nonlinear model itself. The conclusions state that results 'follow a priori expected patterns' and that the model 'cannot account for inaccurate representation of the system dynamics' and is deterministic (climate uncertainty not considered), but with Q2 = no these cannot be credited. Also note the passage says 'daily' rates while the study decides hourly rates.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 and Figures 5-8 report the authors' own optimisation model runs including cases with saline initial soil and/or saline irrigation water, showing simulated root-zone salinity trajectories under the optimal control sequences.
rows.notes: Soil salinity control is simulated only: cases 2-5 show the controller leaching salts with salt-free water (initial 3000 mg/L reduced within 15-30 days using 117 cm water, 100 cm percolation) or stabilising salinity at 1000 mg/L with >120 cm of irrigation. These are outputs of a lumped mass-balance model with no comparison to observed soil salinity, so they do not count as own evidence on the soil-health effect under the rating rules. The study itself acknowledges the model is a conceptualisation subject to revision and that uncertainty in climatic inputs is not considered.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references and appendix); figures are rendered as garbled axis labels but the text describing results is intact. The study is a deterministic optimal-control modelling paper with no field or observational data of its own; all claimed effects are model outputs not validated against measurements.
